title: Three kinds of people
hook: three ways people deal with an attachment

segments.voice: Yesterday, two standards: riches, honor, pride, or poverty, insult, humility, each starting with a small first step. Your line was under his standard. Which small step did you let go by? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

Three people have each come into a large sum of money. Not stolen. Not quite clean either: they got it, Ignatius says, not purely for the love of God. And now each one feels the weight of it. Not the money itself, the grip it has on them. All three want to be at peace with God. All three want to be rid of that grip. They even agree on the goal. What separates them is what they actually do next. Ignatius sets them side by side in the second week and lets the one praying watch. Today: three kinds of people.
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, ONE FORTUNE EACH.` → `THE WEIGHT IS THE GRIP.` → `SAME GOAL, THREE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The first person wants to be free of the attachment. Really wants it. But never takes the means. Next month. After this busy stretch. Ignatius says they put it off right up to the hour of death. The second person also wants to be free, but on one condition: keeping the money. They'd like God to come around to what they've already decided. They'll pray about it, as long as the answer is yes. The third person wants to be free in a different way. They don't cling to keeping it, and they don't cling to giving it up. They want to keep it or let it go only as God moves them and as serves God better. And while they wait to see which, they live as if they'd already let it go in their heart. Look closely at the third. That person might keep the money. The meditation isn't about the money. It's about who holds whom. Jesus puts the same thing in one line, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Ignatius adds an honest note for anyone who notices resistance. If you feel a pull against letting go, he says, ask in prayer for exactly the thing you resist, even against your own inclination. He doesn't pretend the third way is easy. And the meditation ends with the same three conversations as yesterday's. Away from the retreat, the three are easy to spot, and not only around money. A phone, a grudge, a role at work that has become who you are. One says someday. One bargains. One opens the hand and waits.
screen: `THE FIRST: SOMEDAY.` · `THE SECOND: ONLY IF I KEEP IT.` · `THE THIRD: AS GOD MOVES ME.` · `WHO HOLDS WHOM?` · then, large: `WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the third way. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one attachment: something you own, a role you play, a habit, a plan you've already made up your mind about. Ask, honestly, which of the three you are with it right now. The one who'll get to it someday. The one who's bargaining. Or the one who's free. No grade. Then, for this sit, try the third way. Hold it with an open hand, neither clutching it nor throwing it away. If you pray, you can ask God to move you whichever way serves. The bell holds the time.
Three kinds of people. One puts it off, one bargains, and one wants only what serves God, keep it or not. Today's word.
Your line: really free. Today, catch one moment of bargaining, I'll let go if I can keep it, and say the line to yourself instead. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In the second week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray the meditation on the three classes of people after the two standards, using it to test how free they are before making a choice.

original.note: Spanish: Ignatius's own heading for the three kinds of people, rendered in English as three classes or three pairs.

trapdoor: what you thought: three personality types.
what it means: three ways of dealing with an attachment: put it off, bargain, or become really free.
what a scholar hears: it follows the two standards in the second week, is prayed with the same three colloquies, and comes with a note for anyone who resists letting go.

notes: Claims rule: the text's sum ('ten thousand ducats') is given only as 'a large sum of money'.

Paraphrases of nos. 153–155 (the three classes) and no. 157 (asking for what one feels repugnance to, even against the flesh); confirm. The script widens the application beyond money ('a phone, a grudge, a role at work'); confirm this is fair to the meditation.
'Prayed with the same three colloquies' follows no. 156; confirm.
Original: Spanish 'tres binarios' and the English renderings 'classes' or 'pairs'; confirm. Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 6:21 to confirm.
